title: 宋史 490, 外國六, 拂菻 — the Song History on Fulin: the embassy of 1081 from a king whose name ends in 改撒, and the two embassies of 1091. THE LATEST ROMAN CONTACT IN THIS CORPUS, four hundred years after everything else East Asia holds.
language_note:
Literary Chinese, `lzh`, as the corpus's six other East Asian source-language records carry it. `classify_original` returns `('verbatim_original', 'lzh', True)`; `non_latin_ratio` is 1.0, so the `english_marker_ratio` branch that governs romanised records does not apply here at all.

AND THAT SAMENESS IS THIS RECORD'S ONE WEAKNESS, STATED AT THE TOP. East Asia now holds SEVEN source-language records and every one of them is Literary Chinese. The slot was to have been a Turfan Manichaean text in Middle Persian or Parthian — see `notes` for why it is not, and for what was searched.
date: The events are dated by the text itself: 元豐四年十月, the tenth month of the fourth year of Yuanfeng, and 元祐六年, the sixth year of Yuanyou. The translation renders these November 1081 CE and 1091 CE. THE COMPILATION IS LATER AND IS OUTSIDE THIS PROJECT'S WINDOW: the 宋史 was completed in 1345 under Toqto'a, whose name the Siku Quanshu recension prints as 托克托 on this juan's own title page. **The window rule is applied to the EVENTS and to the embassies the text records, not to the date of the compilation** — the same position `eastasia-06-cefu-yuangui` stands on, a 1013 encyclopedia recording a 643 embassy. Stated here rather than assumed, because 1081 and 1091 are the latest dates any record in this corpus carries and they sit barely a century inside the 1204 boundary.
original_text_excerpt: 拂菻國東南至滅力沙北至海皆四十程西至海三十程東自西大食及于闐回紇青唐乃抵中國歴代未嘗朝貢元豐四年十月其王滅力伊靈改撒始遣大首領你厮都令厮孟判來獻鞍馬刀劔眞珠言其國地甚寒土屋無瓦産金銀珠西錦牛羊馬獨峯駞梨杏千年棗巴欖粟麥以蒲萄釀酒樂有箜篌壺琴小簟篥偏鼓王服紅黄衣以金線織絲布纒頭嵗三月則詣佛寺坐紅床使人舁之貴臣如王之服或青綠緋白粉紅黄紫竝纒頭跨馬城市田野皆有首領主之每嵗惟夏秋兩得奉給金錢錦榖帛以治事大小為差刑罰罪輕者杖數十重者至二百大罪則盛以毛囊投諸海不尚鬬戰鄰國小有爭但以文字來徃相詰問事大亦出兵鑄金銀為錢無穿孔面鑿彌勒佛背為王名禁民私造元祐六年其使兩至詔别賜其玉帛二百匹白金瓶襲衣金束帶
original_text_note:
Verbatim Literary Chinese, 295 characters, from Kanripo `raw.githubusercontent.com/kanripo/KR2a0032/master/KR2a0032_490.txt`, read on 2026-09-06. The span runs from 拂菻國東南至滅力沙 to 金束帶 and crosses the page boundaries marked `<pb:KR2a0032_WYG_490-28a>` and `<pb:KR2a0032_WYG_490-28b>`.

EDITORIAL ACTS, DECLARED, AND THEY ARE `eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun`'s EXACTLY. Kanripo's `¶` line markers and its `<pb:...>` page markers are removed and the words they split are closed up. No punctuation is added: the source carries none, and the sentence divisions a reader meets in the translation are the translator's.

VERIFIED BY DIGEST, AND THE CLEANING IS INSIDE THE THING VERIFIED. The removal of `¶` and `<pb:...>` was performed in the browser on the live page and again on the bridge on the typed copy, by the same two rules; SHA-256 over the two results agrees at `7ff3f9f7bd71fe23d6e08738…` on 295 characters. **So what is verified is not only the transcription but the edit**, which is the part a curator's eye is worst at checking. Records 44 and 45 verified a paste; this one verifies a transformation.

THE RECENSION IS THE WENYUANGE SIKU QUANSHU AND THE BOUNDARY IS UNCOLLATED. The page marker names it — `WYG` — and the juan's own heading prints 欽定四庫全書. `eastasia-05` records why that matters and the reason applies with more force here: the Qianlong editors are known to have altered passages about foreign peoples, and this is a passage about a foreign people whose ruler's name is transcribed phonetically. No collation against a Zhonghua Shuju edition was performed, because none is openly reachable from this project.
reference_translation: The country of Fu-lin [Byzantium]. South-east of it you go to Mei-lu-ku [Kilikia ("Cilicia")]; north you go to the sea [Black Sea]; both forty days' journey; west you go to the sea [Mediterranean], thirty days' journey; in the east, starting from western Ta-shih, you come to Yu-tien [Khoten], Hui-ho and Ch'ing-t'ang, and finally reach Zhongguo [China]. They have during former dynasties not sent tribute to our court. During the tenth month of the fourth year of the period Yuan-feng [November, 1081 C.E.], their king, Mieh-li-i-ling-kai-sa [Michael VII Parapinaces Caesar], first sent the ta-shou-ling [a high official] Ni-si-tu-ling-si-meng-p'an to offer as tribute saddled horses, sword-blades, and real pearls. He said: the climate of this country is very cold; houses there have no tiles; the products are gold, silver, pearls, western silk cloth, cows, sheep, horses' camels with single humps, pears, almonds, dates, pa-lan [a kind of date], millet, and wheat. They make wine from grapes; their musical instruments are the lute, the hu-ch'in [the "tea-pot-shaped lute"]; the hsiao-pi-li[a kind of flageolet]; and the p'ien-ku ["side drum"]. The king dresses in red and yellow robes, and wears a turban of silken cloth interwoven with gold thread. In the third month every year he goes to the Temple of Fou-shih [ "Temple of Buddha", here meaning either Muhammed or Christ; in other places the Qu'ran is described as Fou-ching".], to sit on a red couch [palanquin?] which he gets the people to lift. His honored servants [ministers, courtiers, priests?] are dressed like the king, but wear blue, green, purple, white mottled, red, yellow, or brown stuff, wear turbans and ride on horseback. The towns and the country districts are each under the jurisdiction of a shou-ling [chief, sheik?]. Twice a year, during the summer and autumn, they must offer money and cloth [chin-ku-po]. In their criminal decisions they distinguish between great and small offences. Light offences are punished by several tens of blows with the bamboo; heavy offences with up to 200 blows; capital punishment is administered by putting the culprit into a feather bag which is thrown into the sea. They are not bent on making war to neighboring countries, and in the case of small difficulties try to settle matters by correspondence; but when important interests are at stake they will also send out an army. They cast gold and silver coins' without holes, however; on the pile they cut the words Mi-le-fou, which is a king's name. The people are forbidden to counterfeit the coin. During the sixth year of Yuan-yu [1091 C.E.] they sent two embassies, and their king was presented, by imperial order, with 200 pieces of cloth, pairs of white gold vases, and clothing with gold bound in a girdle.
reference_translation_note:
The English is Friedrich Hirth's 1885 translation AS MODIFIED BY JEROME S. ARKENBERG, and the modification is the source's own declaration and not this record's inference. The page states it in these words: "Scanned and edited by Dr. Jerome S. Arkenberg, Department of History, California State University Fullerton. The text has been modified by Dr. Arkenberg. [Any modernization © 2000 Jerome S. Arkenberg.]"

WHAT THE MODIFICATION VISIBLY IS, on the evidence of the text itself: the romanisation is partly modernised, and `Zhongguo [China]` stands where an 1885 book would have written China. **THIS RECORD THEREFORE DOES NOT CLAIM TO HOLD HIRTH'S WORDING.** It holds Hirth-as-modified, cited as such. `eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun` went to the page images on archive.org for its Hirth passage and this record did not; both practices now exist in this corpus and the difference is named here rather than left for someone to find.

THE BRACKETS ARE THE EDITORS' AND ARE ALL KEPT, INCLUDING WHERE THEY ARE MALFORMED. `[Kilikia ("Cilicia")]`, `[a high official]`, `[palanquin?]`, `[ministers, courtiers, priests?]`, `[chief, sheik?]` are identifications and queries; `the hsiao-pi-li[a kind of flageolet]` has no space before the bracket; the Fou-shih note opens `[ ` with a space and closes `Fou-ching".]` with a quotation mark inside the bracket; and `They cast gold and silver coins' without holes` carries a stray apostrophe. NONE OF THESE IS REPAIRED. A curator who tidied them would be editing a published translation on their own authority, which is what FINDING 55 forbids, and the corpus would then hold a text no source prints.

ONE DIVERGENCE BETWEEN THE TWO REGISTERS IS RECORDED WITHOUT BEING ADJUDICATED. Where the Chinese has 面鑿彌勒佛背為王名, the English reads "on the pile they cut the words Mi-le-fou, which is a king's name." The translation transcribes 彌勒佛 rather than translating it and attaches the king's name to it. This record NAMES the divergence and does not settle it: it has opened no commentary, no second translation and no numismatic authority, and an alternative this project supplied itself would be worth nothing.

THE BOUNDARY OF THE TRANSLATION SEARCH. What was looked at: this sourcebook, and the two Silk Road Seattle texts this corpus already cites for `eastasia-01-weilue` and `eastasia-02-hou-hanshu`. What was NOT opened for THIS passage: **Hirth's own page images on archive.org**, which `eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun` did open for its passage and which would settle exactly what Arkenberg changed; and **Friedrich Hirth's `Chao Ju-kua` (1911)** and **Emil Bretschneider's `Mediaeval Researches`**, either of which may translate this juan. No claim is made about what any of them says. The search stopped at the electronic text that names its own underlying edition and its own modifier.

TWO SOURCES, TWO POSITIONS, AND THEY ARE RECORDED SEPARATELY BECAUSE THEY ARE DIFFERENT SOURCES.

THE CHINESE TEXT is Kanripo's, which `eastasia-05-liangshu-qin-lun` records as **CC BY-SA 4.0**. This record inherits that reading and did not re-read the licence page; that is stated so that the rights cell can say what it rests on.

THE ENGLISH is the Internet East Asian History Sourcebook's, whose permission statement is quoted verbatim, from the foot of https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/romchin1.html:

"Unless otherwise indicated the specific electronic form of the document is copyright. Permission is granted for electronic copying, distribution in print form for educational purposes and personal use. If you do reduplicate the document, indicate the source. No permission is granted for commercial use of the Sourcebook."

And the modification notice, also verbatim: "Scanned and edited by Dr. Jerome S. Arkenberg, Department of History, California State University Fullerton. The text has been modified by Dr. Arkenberg. [Any modernization © 2000 Jerome S. Arkenberg.]"

THE POSITION IS `permission_stated_no_licence` — the seventh position, added in F6 by `scandinavia-06-tjurko-bracteate` — and it is the right cell for the same reason it was there: **reuse is permitted in prose and no licence is named anywhere reached.** `open_licence_stated` would require a named licence and there is none; `states_no_terms` would be the opposite lie, since the terms are stated and are permissive. The asked-for attribution — "If you do reduplicate the document, indicate the source" — is given in `translation_source` and in `citation`.

UNDER RULING 74 the underlying 1885 work is out of copyright; what is in copyright is Arkenberg's modernisation of 2000, and the four conditions are met on it: the quotation is one section of a sourcebook covering 91 BCE to 1643 CE, bounded by the section itself; the work is fully cited by author, editor, underlying edition and URL; the rights position is stated verbatim above; and the use is non-commercial research, which this source asks for in those words.
findspot: Not applicable — a transmitted text and not an excavated object. The 宋史 was compiled at the Yuan court and this record's witness is the Wenyuange Siku Quanshu recension of the 1780s, served by Kanripo.
notes:
F6, the East Asia `verbatim_with_provenance` slot. **AND IT IS NOT THE RECORD THE HANDOFF DOCUMENT ASKED FOR. That is the point of this note.**

WHAT WAS ASKED FOR AND WHY IT WAS NOT TAKEN — A SEARCHED FAILURE, RECORDED IN FULL. `F6_CURATION_START.md` §3 pointed the slot at a Turfan Manichaean text in Middle Persian or Parthian, which would have been an EAST ASIA record by findspot and would have settled the `M2 I` / `M 5794 I` mis-regioning in one record. The vein was searched on 2026-09-06 and it fails on the TRANSLATION side, not on reachability:

- `parsigdatabase.com` opens completely, as browser pass 2 found, and its Manichaean section carries **59 Middle Persian texts under Boyce 1975's own sigla** — `a`, `aa`, `ad`, `ae`, `aq`, `ar`, `b` … — with a transcription and a translation.
- **The translation is PERSIAN.** The interface says so in its own heading: "Transcription and Persian translation of Middle Persian texts". The five texts the home page lists as carrying an English translation are all Zoroastrian, not Manichaean.
- **`ingest.fidelity.classify_translation` hard-codes `lang = "en"` for every non-pointer translation chunk.** A Persian translation would therefore enter the index declared as English. That is a false claim in the corpus, and it is a defect in the classifier rather than a reason to write the record badly — see the finding raised in `F6_RESULT.md`.
- `titus.uni-frankfurt.de` carries M 2 in its `Mir.Man., ii` and `Mir.Man., iii` concordance — Andreas & Henning, `Mitteliranische Manichaica`, whose translation is German and in copyright. Boyce 1975 and Asmussen 1975 are in copyright and neither is reachable without a login this session cannot use.
- **So no reachable English translation of a Turfan Manichaean text was found, and the tier that needs one could not be built on it.** `derive_tier` is explicit: source-language text with no published translation is `verbatim_machine_english`, and F6 places no such slot.

THE MIS-REGIONING IS SETTLED ANYWAY, AND IT NEVER NEEDED A RECORD. `M2 I` and the banked `M 5794 I` are Turfan finds and are EAST ASIA candidates under this corpus's findspot rule — the rule that makes `eastasia-04-jingjiao-stele` East Asia and not Persia. That is a fact about two BANKED candidates and it is now written where F7 will read it.

WHY THIS TEXT INSTEAD. The corpus's East Asian view of Rome stops in 643 CE, with `eastasia-06-cefu-yuangui` and `eastasia-07-tang-huiyao` on the same embassy. **This record moves it to 1081 and 1091**, four hundred and forty years later and inside the last century and a quarter of this project's window. The embassy it records is Byzantine: 其王滅力伊靈改撒, whose transcription the translation reads as Michael VII, and whose last two characters 改撒 the corpus can now hold beside `persia-06-shahrestaniha`'s `kēsar` and the Ge‘ez `walda Maḥrǝm` behind `africa-01`'s "son of the invincible god Ares". **Three languages, three transcriptions of the same Roman office, and the Chinese one arrives in the eleventh century.**

AND THE TEXT IS NOT ONLY AN EMBASSY NOTICE. It is a description — climate, houses without tiles, gold and silver and西錦, single-humped camels, grape wine, four named musical instruments, the king's gold-threaded turban, a red couch carried by the people, punishment by feather bag thrown into the sea, and coins with no square hole. `eastasia-07-tang-huiyao` describes Fulin in the seventh century; this describes it in the eleventh, and the two are now comparable inside one corpus.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE. F6 carries one `gloss_capable` declaration and ruling 77 spends it on `arabia-07-cih541`. The material is in the chunked fields if F7 wants it: the 彌勒佛 / "Mi-le-fou, which is a king's name" divergence, and the translator's own queries — `[palanquin?]`, `[chief, sheik?]`, `[ministers, courtiers, priests?]` — which are hedges printed inside the translation.

THE SEVENTH LITERARY CHINESE RECORD, AND THAT IS A COST. East Asia's source-language records are now 7 of 7 in one language, while Africa gained its first local language today. A region that speaks in only one language is a narrower witness than its count suggests, and no line in `ingest.verify --state` currently reports it.

subject_places.name: 拂菻 (Fulin) — the country the whole passage describes
subject_places.note: NO ID. `拂菻` is the Chinese name for the Byzantine empire and it is a POLITY, not a settlement; the passage places it by travel times to seas and to 滅力沙, not by naming a city. `eastasia-07-tang-huiyao` carries the same name and the corpus's rule against turning a people or a state into a city point — persia-05, persia-06, scandinavia-06 — applies unchanged. `regional` with a role is what an unplaced focus looks like.

subject_places.name: 中國 — the court the embassies reach, at 乃抵中國
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND THE TEXT NAMES NO CITY. The route runs east from 西大食 through 于闐, 回紇 and 青唐 and 乃抵中國, and the tribute is offered at a court the passage does not locate. The Song capital is not named in these 295 characters and this record does not supply it.

subject_places.name: 于闐 (Khotan), 回紇 and 青唐 — the stages named on the road east
subject_places.note: NO ID, AND THE ENTRY IS DELIBERATELY THREE NAMES IN ONE. The text lists them as a route and not as three separate subjects, and splitting them would assert an ordering and a precision the sentence does not carry. PLACES.md records that `waypoint` carries no ordering; this is the case that shows why that limit matters.
